In situ generation of active motifs on Ni/Al2O3 during partial oxidation of methane to syngas

What the paper asks

论文正文关注的问题需结合全文引言核对。

Methods

To investigate the energy and structural details of methane dissociation on crystal surfaces, periodic self-consistent DFT calculations were performed using the Vienna Ab Initio Simulation Package46. The Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof form of the generalized gradient approximation was employed to describe the exchange-correlation functional47. To accurately include long-range dispersion interactions, which are often crucial in surface interactions, the D3(BJ) dispersion correction was added48,49. The plane-wave cutoff energy was set to 400 eV, while the k-point sampling of the first Brillouin zone was performed using a Gamma point mesh.

The surface models of Ni(111) and NiO(100) were represented by 4 × 4 supercell periodic slabs containing six atomic layers. For geometric optimizations, the bottom two layers were fixed to mimic the bulk structure, whereas the top four layers and all adsorbates were fully relaxed. All the calculations were spin-polarized to account for the magnetism of Ni atoms and the antiferromagnetic nature of NiO. The DFT + U method was applied to describe the NiO system, with a Hubbard U parameter of 5.4 eV for Ni (ref. 50). The convergence criteria for the electronic structure and geometric optimizations were 1 × 10−7 eV and 0.03 eV Å−1, respectively.

The climbing image nudged elastic band (CI-NEB) method51 was utilized to locate the transition state, and its presence was confirmed by frequency analysis showing a single imaginary frequency. For all the CI-NEB calculations, the bottom two layers were fixed while the top four layers and all adsorbates were fully relaxed, consistent with the geometry optimization procedure described above. Vibrational frequencies were computed using numerical force derivatives with a second-order finite difference method and a step size of 0.015 Å. Because the slab structures of the initial state, transition state and final state are very similar on the same surface model, the vibrational contributions from slab atoms are expected to largely cancel out when computing relative Gibbs free energies52. Therefore, in the vibrational analysis, all slab atoms were kept fixed and only the adsorbate atoms were displaced to obtain vibrational frequencies for methane adsorbed states. Because the methane is adsorbed in the initial state, transition state and final state states, its free translational and rotational motions are suppressed upon adsorption. The corresponding degrees of translational and rotational freedom become hindered and are transformed into the low-frequency vibrational modes within the harmonic treatment. Based on these vibrational frequencies, Gibbs free-energy corrections at 923.15 K (650 °C) were evaluated. This computational strategy, which calibrates the calculated values to the experimental temperature, has been used in previous studies52,53. Bader charge analysis54 and local magnetic moments from spin-polarized calculations were used to characterize the effective charge state and spin of Ni in the [Ni O Ni ] motif.

Main findings

This study observes the in situ formation of [Ni1O1Ni4] motifs on NiO surfaces under reaction conditions. These motifs appear to be associated with catalytic activity for POM to syngas, which differs from the conventional interpretation that metallic Ni NPs are the active species. Through a combination of advanced characterization techniques including operando XAS, quasi in situ XPS, ETEM, AC-ESTEM and DFT calculations, we demonstrate that preformed metallic Ni NPs are oxidized to NiO under POM conditions, yet the catalyst exhibits notable performance (92.0% CH4 conversion, 87.0% syngas selectivity at 650 °C). The in situ-generated [Ni1O1Ni4] structure suggested by AC-ESTEM is proposed as the active site, which remakably lowers the C–H activation barrier to 12.5 kcal mol−1, surpassing the activity of metallic Ni(111) or NiO(100). This work not only redefines the active phase in Ni-based POM catalysts but also provides a framework for designing highly efficient catalytic systems for other redox reactions.
